t: First Day Where You Have Been in All the Rooms: First-Arrival DP
o: Starting in room 0 on day 0, each day you move exactly once: an odd visit count at your current room sends you back to nextVisit[i], an even one advances you to i+1. For nextVisit = [0,0] the tour is rooms 0, 0, 1, so day 2 is the answer; for [0,0,2] the tour is 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 2 giving day 6; and [0,1,2,0] tours 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 for day 6 as well. The catch is scale: with n up to 100000 the day labels grow astronomically because each new room forces a full replay of earlier excursions, which is why the answer is requested modulo 10^9 + 7 and day-by-day simulation cannot finish.
k: You can only advance from room i to i+1 after an even number of visits to i, so progress is monotone: every room before your current one has an even visit count.

After the first visit to room i you bounce back to nextVisit[i], where the parity pattern ahead is identical to the one at its own first arrival, so the excursion replays a previously measured stretch of days.
This yields the closed recurrence f[i+1] = 2*f[i] - f[nextVisit[i]] + 2 on first-arrival days f.
Everything is computed modulo 10^9 + 7, and subtractions must be kept non-negative in C++, Java, and JavaScript.

a.i: Just implement the rules: track per-room visit counts and the current room, advancing one day at a time until room n-1 is entered. This is obviously faithful to the statement, but each new room forces a complete re-run of earlier oscillations, so runtimes explode quickly as n grows. It passes small cases but exceeds limits near the constraint ceiling.
s: Keep a visits array and set i = 0, day = 0.
While i is not n-1: increment visits[i].
If visits[i] is odd jump to nextVisit[i]; otherwise move to i+1.
Increment day after each move and return it once room n-1 is reached.
a.t: Exponential in practice since each new room replays all prior excursions, so the day count grows roughly geometrically with n; hopeless for n = 10^5.

a.n: Approach 2: Linear DP over First Arrivals
a.i: Progress is one-directional: you leave room i forever only after an even count there, so consider f[i], the first day room i is visited. On day f[i]+1 you stand at nextVisit[i], and from there the parities of rooms between nextVisit[i] and i match those at the moment nextVisit[i] was first entered, meaning the excursion back to room i takes exactly f[i] - f[nextVisit[i]] days. Adding the bounce-out day and the final advance gives f[i+1] = 2*f[i] - f[nextVisit[i]] + 2, computable left to right under the modulus.
s: Set f[0] = 0 since day 0 begins in room 0.
For each i from 0 to n-2 evaluate f[i+1] = (2*f[i] - f[nextVisit[i]] + 2) mod 10^9 + 7.
Add a multiple of the modulus before taking % so intermediate values stay non-negative outside Python.
Return f[n-1], the first day every room has been visited.
a.t: O(n) with one constant-time recurrence evaluation per room.
a.sp: O(n) for the first-arrival table; random access to f[nextVisit[i]] prevents a simple rolling reduction.

w: Derive the recurrence aloud, since interviewers grade the reasoning about parity replays more than the formula itself. Pitfalls: producing negative residues in C++/Java/JavaScript (add 2*MOD before the %), misreading that the answer equals f[n-1] rather than some global counter, and attempting simulation past tiny n. A good follow-up is reconstructing the actual visiting schedule from f, or discussing what changes if nextVisit could point forward.
